text: Move or resize the element on the drawing so it leaves the wrong zone — free while the plan is still on paper.

Keep the centre of the home open and unweighted — no heavy furniture, no storage, nothing built on it. The Manasara states this directly; it is the one instruction about the centre the texts give in so many words.
Keep the North-East itself light: low furniture, no heavy storage, nothing piled up, and as much daylight as the room allows.
Put the household's heaviest things — the tallest wardrobe, the stored trunks — against the South and West walls, so weight still gathers where the mandala places it.
Wherever the kitchen ends up, set the cooking platform against the South-East corner of that room and stand facing East to cook. The tradition fixes the hearth's own direction, not only the room's.
Keep water and fire apart inside the kitchen — sink and filter towards the North-East side, stove and gas towards the South-East side, not side by side.
Keep the toilet door shut, the room dry and ventilated, and its floor a step higher than the rooms around it. This is 20th-century practice — no classical verse prescribes it.
A rock-salt bowl in the affected corner. 20th-century practice; no textual basis.
Sleep with your head to the South or the East, and never to the North. Of all the direction rules this is the one every school states alike.
Move the bed into the South-West corner of whichever room you sleep in, so the sleeper still rests on the heaviest part of that room.
Have the stair turn clockwise as you climb, and keep the space beneath it open — not closed in as a store or a toilet.
Sit facing East or North at the desk. Which way the person faces is fixed as firmly in the tradition as where the room sits.
Keep only light, seldom-used things in it — no heavy metal, no water drums, nothing stacked high — and keep the floor visible.
Keep the seating towards the North and East half of the room and the heavy pieces against its South and West walls.
Park nose-out and keep the rest of that corner clear rather than using it for storage. 20th-century practice; no classical basis.
Keep a South-West balcony roofed and screened rather than left open, and put the heavier planters and furniture on it.
Give the prayer space its own wall — a full-height cupboard, a shelf run or a service duct between it and the toilet is enough separation.
Give the entrance a raised threshold and keep the approach to it clear, lit and unobstructed. The threshold is a real element in the texts, not a modern addition.
If there is another doorway on the North or East wall, make that the one the household uses every day and keep this one for service.
Leave the ground at the missing North-East corner open, clean and a little lower than the rest — not filled in with a shed, a store or a parked vehicle.
A Tulsi plant near the North-East. Genuinely traditional (unlike money plant or lucky bamboo).
Follow the mandala with water: overhead storage towards the South-West or West, underground water and the borewell towards the North-East, North or East.
Keep heavy trees off the North-East and off the centre — light planting, grass or open ground there instead, and the big canopy to the South or West.
Screen the side the road points at with a boundary wall or a line of planting. Note that the schools disagree on whether the direction of the thrust matters at all.
Turn the mirror so it does not face the bed, or box the beam in behind a false ceiling. Modern practice; no classical basis found for either.
Vastu Shanti / Vastu Puja — the genuine traditional pacification, prescribed in the Mayamatam.
A copper strip along the zone boundary. Modern practice; efficacy not established.
A Vastu pyramid on the wall. 20th-century 'pyramid power'; claims of antiquity are marketing.
